extracted.intended_audience: prospective readers, subscribers, and contributors to The Forerunner (Charlotte Perkins Gilman); readers interested in women's/social reform and magazine submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Published statement of purpose, content policy, advertising rules, and department scope for The Forerunner (monthly magazine by Charlotte Perkins Gilman). It specifies what the magazine publishes, its mission and values, advertising standards, and the expected annual value to subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and authorship of The Forerunner
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a monthly magazine, publishing stories short and serial, article and essay; drama, verse, satire and sermon; dialogue, fable and fantasy, comment and review. It is written entirely by Charlotte Perkins Gilman."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines allowable genres/formats (short stories, serials, essays, drama, verse, satire, sermons, dialogue, fable, fantasy, commentary, reviews) and an explicit authorship policy: the magazine's content is produced solely by the single author/publisher. Submissions policy implication: the magazine does not accept outside-authored material for its main contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine purpose / mission
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is to stimulate thought: to arouse hope, courage and impatience; to offer practical suggestions and solutions, to voice the strong assurance of better living, here, now, in our own hands to make."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial content should aim to provoke thought, inspire optimism and action, propose practical solutions, and communicate a conviction that better living can be achieved immediately through conscious effort. Pieces should be constructive and actionable rather than merely descriptive or despairing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial themes and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is about people, principles, and the questions of every-day life; the personal and public problems of to-day. It gives a clear, consistent view of human life and how to live it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred subject matter centers on practical social questions, human-centered analysis, and consistent moral/intellectual perspectives. Work should connect personal experience to broader social principles and offer guidance for living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of gender and subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will treat all three phases of our existence--male, female and human. It will discuss Man, in his true place in life; Woman, the Unknown Power; the Child, the most important citizen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should address male, female, and general human perspectives, with particular emphasis on re-evaluating women's roles and centering the child's importance. Submissions (or internal pieces) should consider gender roles and child welfare as key lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / economic stance
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a magazine for humanity, and humanity is social. It holds that Socialism, the economic theory, is part of our gradual Socialization, and that the duty of conscious humanity is to promote Socialization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine endorses a socializing, pro-Socialism viewpoint as part of its intellectual stance. Contributions should be compatible with, or at least not hostile to, the magazine's sympathetic view of Socialism and social reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication rationale and target readership
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is published to express ideas which need a special medium; and in the belief that there are enough persons interested in those ideas to justify the undertaking."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine exists to provide a dedicated forum for particular reformist ideas that lack representation elsewhere; content should serve readers seeking sustained, coherent advocacy and analysis of those ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy — endorsement and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the advertising department, under the above heading, will be described articles personally known and used. So far as individual experience and approval carry weight, and clear truthful description command attention, the advertising pages of The Forerunner will be useful to both dealer and buyer. If advertisers prefer to use their own statements The Forerunner will publish them if it believes them to be true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising in the magazine is expected to be based on personal knowledge/use or truthful description; the editorial team will vet advertiser claims and publish third-party advertiser copy only when they judge it truthful. Implicit anti-patterns: misleading or unverifiable claims, disguised puffery without basis, or advertisements incompatible with the magazine's standards of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned content types and recurring features (first year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main feature (new book 'Our Androcentric Culture'), serial novel ('What Diantha Did'), and multiple short articles (listed topics such as "Private Morality and Public Immorality," "The Beauty Women Have Lost," "Our Overworked Instincts," etc.), plus short stories, poems, sermons, comment and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine sets explicit expectations for a mix of long-form works (a new book and serial novel) alongside shorter essays and creative pieces. For contributors or readers, this signals a balance between sustained argument/fiction and frequent shorter items on topical social/domestic themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Problems department scope and answer policy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The department of 'Personal Problems' does not discuss etiquette, fashions or the removal of freckles. Foolish questions will not be answered, unless at peril of the asker."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This department will concentrate on substantive personal/public problems rather than trivial domestic or cosmetic concerns. Questions deemed trivial or frivolous may be refused or answered with censure; askers should pose significant, thoughtful queries about life and social conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription content promise / value proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you take this magazine one year you will have: One complete novel . . . By C. P. Gilman; One new book . . . By C. P. Gilman; Twelve short stories . . . By C. P. Gilman; Twelve-and-more short articles . . . By C. P. Gilman; Twelve-and-more new poems . . . By C. P. Gilman; Twelve Short Sermons . . . By C. P. Gilman ... DON'T YOU THINK IT'S WORTH A DOLLAR?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher promises concrete yearly deliverables and uses this as the subscription sales argument. This functions as both a marketing claim and an internal production standard: the magazine commits to producing a fixed quantity and variety of content annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial refusal of frivolity / seriousness threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Across editorial statements: emphasis on 'stimulate thought', 'practical suggestions and solutions', and refusal to answer 'foolish questions' in Personal Problems; the magazine will not treat trivialities as worthy content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works and inquiries should cross an implicit seriousness threshold: they must engage with practical/social problems, intellectual argument, or meaningful artistic expression. Submissions that focus on fashion, petty etiquette, or mere ornament may be rejected or ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigrammatic duties of motherhood (prescriptive criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first duty of a mother is to be a mother worth having. The second duty of a mother is to select a father worth having. The third duty of a mother is to bring up children worth having--and to have children worth bringing up! Motherhood is a personal process, Child-culture is a social process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents a tripartite standard for evaluating maternal responsibility: self-improvement as a parent, prudence/selectivity in partnering, and the social obligation of raising valuable citizens. It also distinguishes individual motherhood from broader child-culture (social systems), suggesting that some duties fall to society rather than solely to mothers.
